Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 80, verses 1–4:

[p-425]

Surah 'Abasa (He Frowned) is Meccan, and it has forty-two verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ ﴿because the blind man came to him﴾ ﴿And what would make you perceive? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ ﴿or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾ ﴿As for one who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾ [80:5] ﴿to him you give attention﴾ [80:6] ﴿though it is not upon you if he does not purify himself﴾ [80:7] ﴿But as for he who came to you striving﴾ [80:8] ﴿while he fears [God]﴾ [80:9] ﴿from him you are distracted﴾ [80:10] ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder﴾ [80:11] ﴿So whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12] ﴿in honored scriptures﴾ [80:13] ﴿exalted and purified﴾ [80:14] ﴿[carried] by the hands of scribes﴾ [80:15] ﴿noble and dutiful﴾ [80:16] ﴿Destroyed is man; how disbelieving is he!﴾ [80:17] ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [80:18] ﴿From a sperm-drop He created him and determined him﴾ [80:19] ﴿Then the way He made easy for him﴾ [80:20] ﴿Then He causes him to die and buries him﴾ [80:21] ﴿Then when He wills, He resurrects him﴾ [80:22] ﴿No! He has not fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ [80:23] ﴿Let man look at his food﴾ [80:24] ﴿that We poured down water in torrents﴾ [80:25] ﴿then We split the earth in splitting﴾ [80:26] ﴿and caused to grow therein grain﴾ [80:27] ﴿and grapes and herbage﴾ [80:28] ﴿and olives and palm trees﴾ [80:29] ﴿and gardens of dense trees﴾ [80:30] ﴿and fruit and grass﴾ [80:31] ﴿as provision for you and your livestock﴾ [80:32] ﴿So when the Deafening Blast comes﴾ [80:33] ﴿the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [80:34] ﴿and his mother and his father﴾ [80:35] ﴿and his wife and his children﴾ [80:36] ﴿For every man that Day will have a matter that will occupy him﴾ [80:37] ﴿[Some] faces, that Day, will be bright﴾ [80:38] ﴿laughing, rejoicing﴾ [80:39] ﴿And [other] faces, that Day, will have upon them dust﴾ [80:40] ﴿covered by darkness﴾ [80:41] ﴿Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ [80:42]

Tasaddā (تَصَدّى): ta'arraḍa (he presented himself, paid attention). al-Ra'i said:

"He gave attention to Wiḍāḥ, whose forehead is like a lamp of the dark night, to whom bracelets are brought."

Its origin is tasaddada, from al-ṣadad (صَدَدُ), which is what confronts you and stands opposite you. One says: "My house is ṣadad his house," i.e., opposite it. It was also said that it is from al-ṣadā (الصَّدى), meaning thirst. It was said too that it is from al-ṣadā, the echo you hear when you speak from a distance in an empty place such as a mountain. Al-muṣādāh (المُصاداةُ) means opposition.

Al-safara (السَّفَرَةُ): the scribes, singular sāfir. Safarat al-mar'a (سَفَرَتِ المَرْأةُ) means she unveiled her face (kashafat al-niqāb). Safartu bayna al-qawm asfiru sifāratan (سَفَرْتُ بَيْنَ القَوْمِ أسْفِرُ سِفارَةً) means I reconciled between them, as al-Farrā' said. The singular is safīr and the plural is sufarā'. The poet said:

"So I do not abandon reconciliation among my people, and I do not walk with deceit when I walk."

Al-qaḍb (القَضْبُ): al-Khalīl said: al-faṣfaṣa al-raṭba (الفَصْفَصَةُ الرَّطْبَةُ) is fresh clover, and it is also said with a sīn. When it dries it is called al-qatt. He said: al-qaḍb is a name applied to what grows from the branches of a tree, to be made into arrows or bows.

Al-ghulb (الغُلْبُ) is the plural of ghalbā' (غَلْباءَ). One says ḥadīqa ghalbā' (حَدِيقَةٌ غَلْباءُ), meaning a garden of thick trees, dense and intertwined. Ightalbala al-'ushb (اغْلَوْلَبَ العُشْبُ) means the grass grew and its parts intertwined. Rajul aghlab (رَجُلٌ أغْلَبُ) means a man with a thick neck. The original use of this description is for necks, and from it is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"Thick-necked men run with them, as if they were full-grown camels clothed in hair-cloaks."

Al-abb (الأبُّ): pasture, because it is sought (yu'abb), meaning it is aimed for and visited. Al-abb and al-umm (الأُمُّ) are two brothers in meaning. The poet said:

"Our root is Qays, and Najd is our abode, and for us are the pasture and the watering place."

It was also said that what human beings eat of plants is called al-ḥaṣīd (الحَصِيدَ), and what others eat is called al-abb. From this is the saying of a Companion praising the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

"For him is a blessed supplication, whose wind is the east wind, by which God makes the ḥaṣīda and the abb grow."

Al-ṣākhkha (الصّاخَّةُ): al-Khalīl said: a cry that deafens the ears (taṣukku al-ādhān ṣakkan), meaning it deafens them because of its severe impact. It was also said that it is derived from ṣakkahu bi'l-ḥajar (صَكَّهُ بِالحَجَرِ), when one strikes something with a stone. Al-Zamakhsharī said: asākha li-ḥadīthihi (أصاخَ لِحَدِيثِهِ) is like asākha lahu (أصاخَ لَهُ), both meaning he listened attentively.

Al-ghabara (الغَبَرَةُ): dust. Al-qatara (القَتَرَةُ): blackness like smoke. Abu 'Ubayda said: in the speech of the Arabs, al-qatar means dust, the plural of qatara. Al-Farazdaq said:

"Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a host above whom you see banners and dust."

He has not fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ [80:23] ﴿Let man look at his food﴾ [80:24] ﴿that We poured down water in torrents﴾ [80:25] ﴿then We split the earth in splitting﴾ [80:26] ﴿and caused to grow therein grain﴾ [80:27] ﴿and grapes and herbage﴾ [80:28] ﴿and olives and palm trees﴾ [80:29] ﴿and gardens of dense trees﴾ [80:30] ﴿and fruit and grass﴾ [80:31] ﴿as provision for you and your livestock﴾ [80:32] ﴿So when the Deafening Blast comes﴾ [80:33] ﴿the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [80:34] ﴿and his mother and his father﴾ [80:35] ﴿and his wife and his children﴾ [80:36] ﴿For every man that Day will have a matter that will occupy him﴾ [80:37] ﴿[Some] faces, that Day, will be bright﴾ [80:38] ﴿laughing, rejoicing﴾ [80:39] ﴿And [other] faces, that Day, will have upon them dust﴾ [80:40] ﴿covered by darkness﴾ [80:41] ﴿Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ [80:42].

This surah is Meccan. Its occasion of revelation was the coming of Ibn Umm Maktum to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the scholars of hadith and of tafsir (exegesis) have mentioned his story. They were the people with whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to speak privately about the matter of Islam, namely 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Abu Jahl, Ubayy, and Umayya, and he would invite them to it.

He, al-Ḥasan, Abu 'Imran al-Jawnī, and 'Īsā recited أآنْ (a-'an) with a hamza followed by an alif of extension. Some readers recited it with two clear hamzas. The use of the third-person pronoun in عَبَسَ وتَوَلّى ('abasa wa-tawallā) is a mark of reverence for him, peace be upon him, and of gentleness toward him, so that God does not address him in the second person, because of what direct address with the taa' of the second person carries that is not hidden. The phrase الأعْمى (al-a'mā, "the blind man") was used to indicate what suits gentleness toward him and considerateness toward what he seeks. Ibn 'Atiyya has a discussion here which I have entirely set aside.

The pronoun in لَعَلَّهُ (la'allahu) refers to "the blind man," meaning he purifies himself by what he receives of knowledge, or يَذَّكَّرُ (yadhdhakkaru): he is admonished, so that فَتَنْفَعَهُ ذِكْراكَ (fatanfa'ahu dhikrāka) means your reminder, that is, your admonition, benefits him. The apparent reading is that يُدْرِيكَ (yudrīka) is in the accusative as part of a clause of hope, so the meaning is: you do not know what is hoped for from him, of purification or of remembrance. It was also said that the meaning is: what informs you of his affair and the outcome of his state?

Then the speech begins anew with لَعَلَّهُ يَزَّكّى (la'allahu yazzakkā), meaning his blessing grows and he purifies himself for God. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It was said that the pronoun in لَعَلَّهُ refers to the disbeliever, meaning: you hoped that he would purify himself through Islam, or be reminded so that the reminder would bring him close to accepting the truth, and what informs you that what you hoped for will come about? End of quote. This is an interpretation from which the Qur'an should be kept free.

The majority recited أوْ يَذَّكَّرُ (aw yadhdhakkaru) with shadda on the dhāl and the kāf, originally yatadhakkaru, which was assimilated. Al-A'raj and 'Āṣim in one narration recited يَذْكُرُ (yadhkuru) with a sukūn on the dhāl and a ḍamma on the kāf. The majority recited فَتَنْفَعُهُ (fatanfa'uhu) with a ḍamma on the 'ayn, conjoined to أوْ يَذَّكَّرُ (aw yadhdhakkaru). 'Āṣim in the well-known narration, al-A'raj, Abu Ḥaywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and al-Za'farānī recited it with a fatḥa on both. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is in answer to a tamannī (wish), because أوْ يَذَّكَّرُ (aw yadhdhakkaru) has the same ruling as لَعَلَّهُ يَزَّكّى (la'allahu yazzakkā). This is not a wish; it is a tarajjī (hope), and there is a difference between tarajjī and tamannī. Al-Zamakhsharī said: in the accusative as an answer to la'alla, as in His saying "that I may look at the God of Moses" [40:37]. According to the Basran grammarians, tarajjī has no answer, so the verb is in the accusative by an implied أنْ (an) after the فاء (fā'). As for the Kufan grammarians, they say that it is in the accusative as the answer of tarajjī. We have already discussed this in His saying "that I may look at the God of Moses" [40:37] in the reading of Ḥafṣ, and we explained the Basran position on the accusative of the imperfect verb.

They were the people with whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to speak privately about the matter of Islam, namely 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Abu Jahl, Ubayy, and Umayya, and he would invite them to it.

أنْ جاءَهُ (an jā'ahu) is a maf'ūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), meaning "because he came to him." It is linked to تَوَلّى (tawallā) according to the preference of the Basran grammarians in matters of government (al-a'māl), and to عَبَسَ ('abasa) according to the preference of the Kufan grammarians.

The majority of readers recited عَبَسَ ('abasa) without shadda and أنْ (an) with a single hamza. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited it with a shadda on the bā' (عَبَّسَ). He, al-Ḥasan, Abu 'Imran al-Jawnī, and 'Īsā recited أآنْ (a-'an) with a hamza followed by an alif of extension. Some readers recited it with two clear hamzas. The hamza in these two readings is interrogative, and in both one pauses at تَوَلّى (tawallā). The meaning is: "Because he came to him, [would you] do such-and-such?" The use of the third-person pronoun in عَبَسَ وتَوَلّى ('abasa wa-tawallā) is a mark of reverence for him, peace be upon him, and of gentleness toward him, so that God does not address him in the second person, because of what direct address with the taa' of the second person carries that is not hidden. The phrase الأعْمى (al-a'mā, "the blind man") was used to indicate what suits gentleness toward him and considerateness toward what he seeks. Ibn 'Atiyya has a discussion here which I have entirely set aside.

The pronoun in لَعَلَّهُ (la'allahu) refers to "the blind man," meaning he purifies himself by what he receives of knowledge, or يَذَّكَّرُ (yadhdhakkaru): he is admonished, so that فَتَنْفَعَهُ ذِكْراكَ (fatanfa'ahu dhikrāka) means your reminder, that is, your admonition, benefits him. The apparent reading is that يُدْرِيكَ (yudrīka) is in the accusative as part of a clause of hope, so the meaning is: you do not know what is hoped for from him, of purification or of remembrance. It was also said that the meaning is: what informs you of his affair and the outcome of his state?

Then the speech begins anew with لَعَلَّهُ يَزَّكّى (la'allahu yazzakkā), meaning his blessing grows and he purifies himself for God. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It was said that the pronoun in لَعَلَّهُ refers to the disbeliever, meaning: you hoped that he would purify himself through Islam, or be reminded so that the reminder would bring him close to accepting the truth, and what informs you that what you hoped for will come about? End of quote. This is an interpretation from which the Qur'an should be kept free.

The majority recited أوْ يَذَّكَّرُ (aw yadhdhakkaru) with shadda on the dhāl and the kāf, originally yatadhakkaru, which was assimilated. Al-A'raj and 'Āṣim in one narration recited يَذْكُرُ (yadhkuru) with a sukūn on the dhāl and a ḍamma on the kāf. The majority recited فَتَنْفَعُهُ (fatanfa'uhu) with a ḍamma on the 'ayn, conjoined to أوْ يَذَّكَّرُ (aw yadhdhakkaru). 'Āṣim in the well-known narration, al-A'raj, Abu Ḥaywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and al-Za'farānī recited it with a fatḥa on both. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is in answer to a tamannī (wish), because أوْ يَذَّكَّرُ (aw yadhdhakkaru) has the same ruling as لَعَلَّهُ يَزَّكّى (la'allahu yazzakkā). This is not a wish; it is a tarajjī (hope), and there is a difference between tarajjī and tamannī. Al-Zamakhsharī said: in the accusative as an answer to la'alla, as in His saying "that I may look at the God of Moses" [40:37]. According to the Basran grammarians, tarajjī has no answer, so the verb is in the accusative by an implied أنْ (an) after the فاء (fā'). As for the Kufan grammarians, they say that it is in the accusative as the answer of tarajjī. We have already discussed this in His saying "that I may look at the God of Moses" [40:37] in the reading of Ḥafṣ, and we explained the Basran position on the accusative of the imperfect verb.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 80, verses 5–16:**

﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾. Its apparent meaning is one who has wealth and riches. Al-Kalbi said: "Self-sufficient of Allah." It was also said: "Self-sufficient of faith in Allah." It has been said: "To take it to mean wealth does not befit the rank of prophethood, and what indicates this is that if it meant wealth, the counterpart would be: *﴿But as for him who comes to you eager (in faith)﴾*, [and] *﴿poor and humble﴾*." Al-Hasan, Abu Raja, Qatadah, al-A'raj, Isa, al-A'mash and the majority of the Seven Readers (al-sab'ah, the seven canonical readers) read *tasaddaa* (تَصَدّى) with a light *sad*. Its original form is *yatasaddaa*, and one letter was elided. The two Haramayn (the Meccan and Medinan readers) read it with a doubled *sad*, assimilating the *ta'* into the *sad*. Abu Ja'far read *tusaddaa* (تُصَدّى) with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a light *sad*, meaning: your eagerness for his conversion turns you away. It is said: *tusadda al-rajul* and *sadday-tuhu*. The one who considers himself self-sufficient is al-Walid, or Umayyah, or Utbah and Shaybah, or Umayyah [alone], or all those mentioned in the occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul); these are the opinions. Al-Qurtubi said: "All of this is an error by the exegetes (mufassirun), because Umayyah and al-Walid were in Mecca, while Ibn Umm Maktum was in Medina and was not present with them, and they both died as disbelievers, one before the Hijrah and the other at Badr. Umayyah never intended to go to Medina, and he was never present with him, either alone or with anyone else." End of quote. The error lies with al-Qurtubi: how can he deny that Ibn Umm Maktum was present with them? This is his own delusion, for they were all from Quraysh, and Ibn Umm Maktum was there [in Mecca]. The whole surah is Meccan by consensus. How can he say, "Ibn Umm Maktum was in Medina"? He was first in Mecca, then migrated to Medina, and they were all in Mecca at the time of the revelation of this verse. Ibn Umm Maktum is Abd Allah ibn Sarh ibn Malik ibn Rabi'ah al-Fihri, from the Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy. His mother, Umm Maktum, was the mother of his father, Atikah, and he was the maternal cousin of Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her).

(p-428) ﴿And what is it to you if he does not purify himself?﴾ This is a belittling of the disbeliever's matter and an urging to turn away from him and to stop caring about him. That is: what does it matter to you that he does not prosper and is not purified from the filth of disbelief? ﴿But as for him who comes to you eagerly﴾, meaning he walks swiftly in matters of his religion. ﴿And he fears﴾, meaning he fears Allah, or fears the disbelievers and their harm, or fears stumbling and falling because he is blind, and he came without a guide to lead him. *Talahha* (تَلَهّى): one is occupied; it is said: *lahā 'an al-shay'* (لها عَنِ الشَّيْءِ يَلَهّى) when one is distracted from something. It has been said: this is not from *al-lahw* (play, idle diversion), which is from the *waw*-root. It is possible that it is from it, because what is formed on the pattern *fa'ila* from a *waw*-root and whose *waw* becomes *ya'* due to the preceding *kasra*, as in *shaqiya yashqa* (he suffered). If its verbal noun comes with a *ya'*, then it is from a root other than the root of *lahw*. The majority read *talahha*, and al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read *'anhu tallaha* (عَنْهُوتَّلَهّى) with the assimilation of the present-tense *ta'* into the *ta'* of *tafa''ala*. Abu Ja'far read it with a *damma*, in the passive voice, meaning: the disbeliever's call to Islam distracts you. Talhah read it with two *ta'*s, and from him also [a reading] with one *ta'* and a sukun on the *lam*.

﴿Nay, indeed it﴾, that is, the surah of the Qur'an and its verses, ﴿is a reminder﴾, an admonition from which one benefits. ﴿So whoever wills, let him remember it﴾, that is, whoever wills to remember this admonition, let him remember it. The pronoun is in the masculine because *al-tadhkirah* is *al-dhikr* (remembrance). This is a parenthetical clause containing promise and warning: ﴿Whoever wills, takes a path to his Lord﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]. It is inserted between *tadhkirah* and its description, meaning: a reminder which is [existing] ﴿in scriptures﴾. It was said: the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). It was said: the scriptures of the saints (awliya') that were sent down. It was said: the scriptures of the Muslims, in which case it is a report of the unseen, since the Qur'an was not written in scriptures during the time of his peace be upon him in Mecca when the Qur'an was being revealed to him. ﴿Exalted﴾ with Allah, and ﴿raised high﴾ in the seventh heaven; this was said by Yahya ibn Salam. Or it is ﴿raised high﴾ above doubts and contradiction, or raised high in status. ﴿Purified﴾, meaning free from every impurity; this was said by al-Hasan. He also said: purified from being sent down to the polytheists. Al-Zamakhshari said: exempt from the hands of the devils; no one touches it except the hands of purified angels. ﴿Scribes﴾, writers who copy the books from the Preserved Tablet. End of quote.

﴿By the hands of scribes﴾. Ibn Abbas said: they are the angels, because they are writers. He also said: because they travel (yasfirun) between Allah the Exalted and His prophets. Qatadah said: they are the reciters, and the singular of *safarah* is *safir*. Wahb said: they are the Companions, because some of them travel (yasfiru) to others for goodness, teaching and knowledge.

(Killed is man; how disbelieving he is!) It was said: this was revealed concerning Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, who had alienated his father and then embraced Islam. His father then sought to reconcile with him, gave him wealth, and equipped him for travel to Syria. Utbah sent word to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he disbelieved in the Lord of the star when it sets. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, send Your dog upon him to devour him." When Utbah reached al-Ghadirah, he recalled the supplication, so he promised those with him a thousand dinars if he woke up alive. They made him sleep in the middle of the caravan, with the baggage around him. A lion came up to the saddlebags, leapt, and was upon him, and it tore him apart. His father would lament him and weep over him, and he said: "Muhammad has never said anything at all but that it came to pass." Even though the verse was revealed concerning a particular person, "man" (al-insan) is intended to mean the disbeliever in general. "Killed" (qutila) is an invocation against him, and killing is the greatest of the hardships of this world.

"How disbelieving he is!" The apparent meaning is an expression of wonder (ta'ajjub) at the extent of his disbelief. Such wonder is attributed to created beings, since it is impossible with respect to Allah, the Exalted; that is, he is among those of whom it is said, "How disbelieving he is!" It was also said that ma is an interrogative of reproach (istifham tawqif), meaning: "What thing made him disbelieve?" That is, "What made him a disbeliever?" In the sense of: "For what reason is it permissible for him to disbelieve?"

"From what thing did He create him?" This is an interrogative in the sense of establishing the lowliness of that from which he was created. Then He specified that thing, saying: ﴿From a drop of sperm He created him and proportioned him.﴾ That is, He prepared him for what suits him. Ibn Abbas said: that is, in the womb of his mother. And it is related from him that He proportioned his limbs, and [made him] handsome or ugly, short or tall, wretched or happy. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ata', and Ibn Abbas in a narration from Abu Salih said: "the way" is a general noun covering both guidance and misguidance; that is, He facilitated for some people this (path), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾ [al-Insan: 3], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We showed him the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. And it is related from Ibn (p. 429) Abbas: He facilitated for him his exit from his mother's womb.

"Then He caused him to die and assigned him a grave." That is, He made for him a grave to protect his body from being eaten by birds and beasts. Qabara means he buried him, and aqbara means he made him such that he is buried and assigned him a grave. The qabir is one who buries with his own hand. Al-A'sha said:

"Had you propped a dead man against her grave, he would have lived and not been carried off to the gravedigger."

"Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him." That is, when He wills to raise him, He raises him. The meaning is: when the time that Allah has willed arrives, which is the Day of Resurrection. In the book al-Lawami': Shu'ayb ibn al-Hibhab read shaa nashrahu without a hamza before the nun, and both are dialects for revival. In the book of Ibn Atiyyah: Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamzah read shaa nashrahu.

"No!" This is a rebuke to man for what he is in of disbelief and transgression. ﴿He has not fulfilled what He commanded him.﴾ That is, from the beginning of the period of his obligation until the time of his burial, he has not carried out what Allah, the Exalted, commanded him. The pronoun in yaqdi refers to man. Ibn Furak said it refers to Allah, the Exalted: that is, Allah has not decreed for this disbeliever what He commanded him of faith; rather, He commanded him with what He did not decree for him.

When He had enumerated His blessings in man himself, He mentioned the blessings in that by which his life is sustained, and commanded him to look at his food and the states that went into his food until it became ready to be eaten. The apparent meaning is that "food" is the thing eaten, and how Allah, the Exalted, facilitates it through these mentioned intermediaries: pouring water, splitting the earth, and causing growth. This is the view of the majority. Ubayy, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others said: ﴿to his food﴾ means when it becomes waste, so that he may reflect on the outcome of the world, and on what its people perish for.

The majority read innā (with a kasra on the hamza), while al-A'raj, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, the Kufans, and Ruways read annā (with a fatha on the hamza), and al-Husayn ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read annī with a fatha on the hamza and imala. The kasra is for a resumptive sentence (istinaf) in listing the ways of reaching food; the fatha, they said, is a substitute (badal). Some rejected this, because the second is not the first. It was said: it is not as they rejected, because the meaning is: "Let man look at Our bounty in his food," so the substitution is correct and valid. End of quote. It is as if they made it a badal al-kull min al-kull (substitution of a whole for a whole). What appears to be correct is that it is a badal al-ishtimal (partial substitution, where the second term is connected to the first). The reading of Ubayy with imala is in the sense of: "Let man look at how We poured," and Allah, the Exalted, attributed the pouring and the splitting to Himself, as one attributes an act to its cause. The pouring of water is the rain. The apparent meaning is that the splitting is a metaphor for the farmer's splitting of the soil by the means customary for it. It was also said: the splitting of the earth is by the plants.

﴿Grain﴾: this includes what is called grain, such as wheat, barley, maize, sult, lentils, and other things. ﴿And fodder﴾: al-Hasan said: it is fodder, and the people of Makkah call alfalfa (qatt) qadb. It was also said: it is clover (fasfasah), but this was weakened because it is included under abb. It was also said: it is the tender plants that a son of Adam cuts to eat, such as vegetables and herbs. Ibn Abbas said: it is fresh dates, because it is cut from the palm, and because He mentioned grapes before it. ﴿Thick-trunked﴾: Ibn Abbas said: thick. It is also related from him: tall. From Qatadah and Ibn Zayd: noble. ﴿And fruit﴾: what people eat of the fruit of trees, such as plums and figs.

﴿And pasture﴾: what animals eat of the grass. Al-Dahhak said: the chaff only. Al-Kalbi said: every plant other than fruit, its fresh part, and abb is its dry part.

﴿The Deafening Blast﴾: a name of the Day of Resurrection whose sound deafens the ears. The Arabs say: "The deafening blast struck them, and the calamity befell them," meaning the great disaster. Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: the deafening blast is the one that causes deafness, and yet it is (also) one that makes hear; this is from the wonders of eloquence, like his saying:

"Their secret deafened them in the days of their separation, so have you heard of a secret that causes deafness?"

And the saying of another:

"The mourner deafened you to him, though he was the more audible."

By the life of Allah, the cry of the Resurrection makes hear, deafening one to the world and making one hear the affairs of the Hereafter. End of quote.

﴿On the day a man flees﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "when," and the response of "when" is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Every person will be preoccupied with himself," which is indicated by: ﴿For every man among them, that Day, there will be a matter that preoccupies him.﴾ His fleeing is from the intensity of the terror of the Day of Resurrection, as came in the saying of the Messengers: "Myself, myself." (Killed is man; how disbelieving he is!) It was said: this was revealed concerning Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, who had alienated his father and then embraced Islam. His father then sought to reconcile with him, gave him wealth, and equipped him for travel to Syria. Utbah sent word to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he disbelieved in the Lord of the star when it sets. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, send Your dog upon him to devour him." When Utbah reached al-Ghadirah, he recalled the supplication, so he promised those with him a thousand dinars if he woke up alive. They made him sleep in the middle of the caravan, with the baggage around him. A lion came up to the saddlebags, leapt, and was upon him, and it tore him apart. His father would lament him and weep over him, and he said: "Muhammad has never said anything at all but that it came to pass." Even though the verse was revealed concerning a particular person, "man" (al-insan) is intended to mean the disbeliever in general. "Killed" (qutila) is an invocation against him, and killing is the greatest of the hardships of this world.

"How disbelieving he is!" The apparent meaning is an expression of wonder (ta'ajjub) at the extent of his disbelief. Such wonder is attributed to created beings, since it is impossible with respect to Allah, the Exalted; that is, he is among those of whom it is said, "How disbelieving he is!" It was also said that ma is an interrogative of reproach (istifham tawqif), meaning: "What thing made him disbelieve?" That is, "What made him a disbeliever?" In the sense of: "For what reason is it permissible for him to disbelieve?"

"From what thing did He create him?" This is an interrogative in the sense of establishing the lowliness of that from which he was created. Then He specified that thing, saying: ﴿From a drop of sperm He created him and proportioned him.﴾ That is, He prepared him for what suits him. Ibn Abbas said: that is, in the womb of his mother. And it is related from him that He proportioned his limbs, and [made him] handsome or ugly, short or tall, wretched or happy.
